grammar-foundation-hangul-blocks: Korean doesn't write letters in a straight line like English; instead it packs them into square syllable blocks, each holding one initial consonant, one vowel, and an optional final consonant (the 받침). Think of every block as one beat you say out loud: 한 is ㅎ+ㅏ+ㄴ, and 글 is ㄱ+ㅡ+ㄹ, so 한글 is just two beats. The vowel sits to the right of the initial (가) or underneath it (고), depending on the vowel's shape. The common beginner trap is trying to read the letters left-to-right across the whole word; always group them into blocks first, or words like 학교 become unreadable.
grammar-particle-eun-neun: 은/는 attaches to a noun to mark it as the topic, the thing the rest of the sentence is about, roughly like saying 'as for...' in English. Picture it as spotlighting one item and quietly comparing it to others: 저는 학생이에요 means 'as for me, I'm a student,' often hinting 'others might not be.' Use 은 after a final consonant (선생님은) and 는 after a vowel (저는). Beginners overuse it as a plain subject marker, but if you're introducing brand-new information or answering 'who did it?', you usually want 이/가 instead.
grammar-particle-i-ga: 이/가 marks the grammatical subject, especially when something newly appears, exists, happens to you, or is the specific answer to a question. The intuition: 이/가 points a finger and says 'this one, right here,' while 은/는 steps back to set a theme. For example 비가 와요 ('rain is coming') and 누가 왔어요? — 친구가 왔어요 ('who came? a friend came') both spotlight fresh, specific information. Use 이 after a consonant (책이) and 가 after a vowel (친구가); a frequent slip is saying 저가 instead of the irregular 제가 for 'I.'
grammar-particle-eul-reul: 을/를 marks the direct object, the thing that directly receives the action of the verb, answering 'what?' or 'whom?' after a verb. A handy mental model: the object is whatever the verb is 'done to,' so in 물을 마셔요 ('I drink water'), 물 is being drunk. Attach 을 after a final consonant (밥을 먹어요) and 를 after a vowel (커피를 마셔요). In casual speech Koreans often drop this particle entirely (밥 먹어요), so don't panic when you don't hear it, but in writing and clear sentences it's the reliable signal of what's being acted on.
grammar-particle-e: 에 is a quiet, all-purpose particle for time, a destination you're heading to, and the location where something simply exists. Think of it as pinning a noun to a point on a map or a clock: 학교에 가요 ('I go to school'), 세 시에 만나요 ('let's meet at three'), and 집에 있어요 ('I'm at home'). Notice it marks where something is, not where an action busily happens. The classic mistake is using 에 for the place of an action like eating or studying; for that you need 에서, so 도서관에 공부해요 is wrong and 도서관에서 공부해요 is right.
grammar-particle-eseo: 에서 marks the place where an action actively takes place, and it also means 'from' a starting point. The intuition: if a verb shows real activity happening somewhere, that location takes 에서, as in 카페에서 일해요 ('I work at the cafe') or 식당에서 먹어요 ('I eat at the restaurant'). For the 'from' sense, it shows origin: 한국에서 왔어요 ('I came from Korea'). The key beginner confusion is 에 versus 에서; remember that still existence (있다, 살다 sometimes) tends toward 에, while busy actions take 에서, so you sit 의자에 but study 도서관에서.
grammar-particle-ege-hante: 에게/한테 marks the person (or animal) who receives something, like a gift, a message, or an action directed at them, matching English 'to' someone. Picture an arrow flying toward a recipient: 친구에게 선물을 줬어요 ('I gave a present to my friend') or 엄마한테 전화했어요 ('I called mom'). The two are interchangeable in meaning, but 한테 sounds casual and conversational while 에게 feels a bit more formal or written. Two cautions for beginners: don't use these for places (a destination still takes 에, not 에게), and when speaking to someone you must respect, switch to the honorific form 께 instead.
grammar-particle-ro-euro: This particle marks the means, method, or direction of an action, and also the language something is spoken in. A handy mental model: attach it to a noun and think "by means of / toward / using" that noun. Use 로 after a vowel or ㄹ (버스로 가요 = I go by bus; 집으로 = toward home) and 으로 after other consonants; for language, 한국어로 말해요 = I speak in Korean. The classic pitfall is confusing it with 에 (a fixed destination)—로/으로 stresses the route or tool, not the final spot itself.
grammar-particle-do: 도 means "also," "too," or even "even," piling one more item onto what was already mentioned. Picture stacking things on a tray: whatever 도 attaches to gets added to the list. Crucially, 도 replaces the subject/topic and object particles—so you say 저도 학생이에요 (I'm a student too), never 저는도. Another example: 커피도 좋아요 = I like coffee too. The common beginner slip is keeping 은/는 or 이/가 in front of 도; just drop them and let 도 do the work.
grammar-particle-man: 만 means "only" or "just," narrowing your statement down to one thing and excluding everything else. Think of it as drawing a tight circle around a single noun: nothing else counts. For example 물만 마셔요 = I drink only water, and 한 명만 왔어요 = only one person came. Unlike 도, 만 can sit with some particles (학교에서만 = only at school), but a frequent mistake is forcing 이/가 or 을/를 after it; usually 만 just replaces them, as in 이것만 주세요 = give me just this.
grammar-particle-buteo-kkaji: This pair marks the start and end of a range: 부터 means "from" (a beginning point) and 까지 means "until/to" (an ending point), for both time and place. Imagine drawing a line with a starting dot and a finishing dot. A natural sentence is 아침부터 저녁까지 일해요 = I work from morning until evening. Note that for a starting *place* Korean usually prefers 에서 over 부터 (집에서 학교까지 = from home to school), so the pitfall is overusing 부터 for physical locations.
grammar-ending-want: To say you want to do something, take a verb stem and add 고 싶어요. Mental model: 고 glues onto the action and 싶어요 adds the feeling of "I wish to." For example 먹다 (to eat) becomes 먹고 싶어요 = I want to eat, and 가다 becomes 가고 싶어요 = I want to go. Two pitfalls: this is for *your own* desire with action verbs, not for "I want a thing" (use 원해요 or 필요해요 for nouns), and when talking about someone else's want you switch to 고 싶어해요.
grammar-ending-can: This ending expresses ability or possibility—"can" or "it's possible to." Attach ㄹ 수 있어요 to a stem ending in a vowel and 을 수 있어요 to one ending in a consonant; literally 수 means a "way/method" that 있어요 (exists). For example 할 수 있어요 = I can do it, and 먹을 수 있어요 = I can eat it. To say you can't, flip 있어요 to 없어요 (갈 수 없어요 = I can't go); the common slip is forgetting the space before 수 or mixing up the ㄹ/을 choice.
grammar-ending-mot: 못 goes right before a verb to say you *can't* do something because of a circumstance, lack of skill, or outside obstacle—not because you choose not to. Think of it as a wall blocking the action even though you might want to do it. For example 못 가요 = I can't go (something prevents me), and 수영 못 해요 = I can't swim. Don't confuse 못 with 안, which means you simply *don't* by choice (안 가요 = I'm not going); also note 하다 verbs split, so it's 수영 못 해요, not 못 수영해요.
grammar-ending-must: This ending expresses necessity or obligation — the English "have to" or "must." Picture it as two ideas glued together: "if I do this action, then it's good/okay," so doing the thing is the only acceptable path. For example, 약을 먹어야 해요 means "I have to take my medicine," and 집에 가야 해요 means "I have to go home." A common beginner slip is forgetting the vowel harmony on the stem (가 + 아야 → 가야, not 가어야), and remember that for permission you switch to 아/어도 돼요, not this form.
grammar-ending-permission: Use this to ask for or grant permission — "May I?" or "Is it okay if I...?" The intuition is "even if I do this action, it still turns out fine," so the 도 carries an "even" nuance and 돼요 means "it works / it's okay." You might ask 여기 앉아도 돼요? ("May I sit here?") and hear back 네, 앉아도 돼요 ("Yes, you may sit"). Beginners often confuse this with obligation: 가야 해요 means "I have to go," while 가도 돼요 means "I may go," so don't mix up 야 해요 and 도 돼요.
grammar-ending-request: This is how you politely ask someone to do something for you — "please do (it)." Think of 주세요 as literally "please give me," so you are asking the listener to "give" you the favor of the action. For instance, 잠깐만 기다려 주세요 means "please wait a moment," and 천천히 말해 주세요 means "please speak slowly." Don't confuse this with 주세요 attached to a noun (물 주세요, "water please"); the 아/어 주세요 form needs a verb stem, and avoid it for prohibitions — "please don't" uses 지 마세요 instead.
grammar-ending-prohibition: This ending tells someone politely NOT to do an action — you'll see it on signs and hear it from staff. Mentally, 지 마세요 attaches the "stop/don't" verb 말다 to any action, like putting a red circle over a picture. Common examples are 만지지 마세요 ("please don't touch") and 사진을 찍지 마세요 ("please don't take photos"). A frequent mistake is trying to negate with 안 here — you can't say 안 만지세요 for a command; prohibitions specifically use the 지 마세요 pattern, and note the stem keeps its 지 with no vowel harmony.
grammar-connector-because: This connector links a reason to its result — "because" or "so." Imagine the first clause naturally flowing downhill into the second: the cause comes first, then the effect, with no tense marking on the 아서/어서 part itself. For example, 배가 고파서 밥을 먹었어요 means "I was hungry, so I ate," and 비가 와서 집에 있었어요 means "because it rained, I stayed home." The big pitfall: never use 아서/어서 with commands or suggestions (don't say 피곤해서 쉬세요) — for those reasons you need 으니까 instead.
grammar-connector-and: This connector strings actions or descriptions together — "and" or "and then." Think of 고 as a simple chain link: it can list qualities at the same time (이 방은 크고 밝아요, "this room is big and bright") or put events in sequence (밥을 먹고 학교에 갔어요, "I ate and then went to school"). The key intuition is that 고 stays plain — you don't conjugate tense on it; the final verb carries the tense for the whole sentence. Beginners sometimes reach for 고 to mean "because"; for cause-and-effect you want 아서/어서 instead.
grammar-connector-if: Attach 면 (or 으면 after a consonant) to set up a condition — "if" or "when." The mental model is a doorway: "once this first situation happens, the second part follows." For example, 시간이 있으면 만나요 means "if you have time, let's meet," and 봄이 오면 꽃이 펴요 means "when spring comes, flowers bloom." Note that Korean uses one 면 for both "if" and "when," so context decides; a common slip is forgetting the 으 after a consonant stem (먹다 → 먹으면, not 먹면).
grammar-ending-promise: This ending voices the speaker's own decision or promise — "I will (do it)." The crucial intuition is that it's a commitment made to the listener, often reacting to them, not a neutral forecast about the future. For example, 제가 할게요 means "I'll do it (so don't worry)," and 내일 전화할게요 means "I'll call you tomorrow (I promise)." The classic pitfall is using it for other people or for predictions — you can't say 비가 올게요 for "it will rain"; 을게요 only works with first-person "I," and for plain predictions use 을 거예요 instead.
grammar-modifier-nl: When a describing word sits in front of a noun, Korean changes its ending. The ㄴ/은 form describes how something is right now: 큰 가방 (a big bag), 작은 방 (a small room), 매운 음식 (spicy food). The intuition is a snapshot of the present — so 뜨거운 물 is water that is hot at this moment. Switch to the ㄹ/을 form only for something that will or might become that way later, which is why 뜨거울 물 (water that will get hot) feels different from 뜨거운 물. Watch two traps: ㅂ-irregular adjectives use 운 (맵다 → 매운, not 맵은), and 있다/없다 words use 는 (맛있다 → 맛있는).
grammar-irregular-stems: Most Korean stems just take an ending (먹다 → 먹어요), but a few reshape their last letter before a vowel ending, and that surprises beginners. Four common ones: ㅂ becomes 우 (맵다 → 매워요, 매운), ㄷ becomes ㄹ (듣다 → 들어요), ㅡ simply drops before 아/어 (크다 → 커요, 바쁘다 → 바빠요), and ㄹ-stems drop their ㄹ before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ (살다 → 삽니다, 사는). The safe strategy is to memorize the polite -아/어요 form as your anchor and build outward from it. The change only happens before a vowel ending — before a consonant the stem stays put (듣고, 듣습니다) — so never conjugate them literally as 맵어요 or 듣어요.
